_comment: Dragon's Lair playtest NPCs. This module extends `default`, so the four base NPCs (Elder Marisol, Orin the Smith, the Stranger in Grey, Alric the Armorer) are inherited and not redeclared here. Schema matches default/npcs.json: { id, name, sprite, counter, personal_history, dialogs: [{ id, title, text }] }. Dialog ids are unique within an NPC and stable for quest / script references.

npcs.name: Elder Marisol
npcs.personal_history: Marisol has guided the village of Hollowmere through three generations. Born to a fisher and a herbalist, she trained as a cleric in the mountain monasteries before returning home when her younger sister vanished into the Wandering Wood. She still wears her sister's iron pendant beneath her vestments. Quietly devout, plainly spoken, and slow to anger — but absolute when she's made up her mind.

dialogs.title: First meeting
dialogs.text: Welcome to Hollowmere, travelers. We see few visitors this side of the Wandering Wood. If you mean us no harm, the hearth at the chapel is always lit.

dialogs.title: Warning about the wood
dialogs.text: Don't take the western path after dusk. The trees… remember things. My sister learned that lesson, and the wood kept her in payment.

dialogs.title: Parting words
dialogs.text: May the lantern guide you home. And if you find a girl with an iron pendant out there — bring her back to me.

npcs.name: Orin the Smith
npcs.personal_history: Orin's forge has stood at the crossroads for nineteen years. Before that he served two campaigns under the eastern banner, lost half his left hand to a goblin axe, and decided that hammering iron paid better and hurt less than swinging it. He brags about his beer, dotes on his three daughters, and pretends not to hear when the village asks him to fix things for free.

dialogs.title: Behind the counter
dialogs.text: If it cuts, breaks, or burns, I can fix it. If you can pay. The two go together, friend.

dialogs.title: When asked about the eastern campaign
dialogs.text: I'll tell you this once and never again: the songs lie. There was no glory in those mud trenches. Only the lads who stopped breathing, and the rest of us, who couldn't.

npcs.name: Stranger in Grey
npcs.personal_history: Nobody in Hollowmere knows where the Stranger came from, only that he arrived the same evening Marisol's sister disappeared, and has rented the same back room at the inn ever since. Pays in old coin, drinks alone, watches the western road. The innkeeper thinks he's harmless; the cooper thinks he's a haunt; Marisol won't say.

dialogs.title: First approach
dialogs.text: I'm waiting for someone. They'll come back, eventually. Everyone does, eventually.

npcs.name: Brenna Quill
npcs.personal_history: Brenna's family has poured ale at The Bent Lantern for four generations. She inherited the inn the winter her father took a chill on the dragon road and never warmed up again. She runs a clean common-room, keeps her thumb on every rumor that passes through Hollowmere, and lets the Stranger in Grey have the back room because his coin is old and his silences are quiet. She's lost two cousins to the Wandering Wood and doesn't care who knows she hates the trees.

dialogs.title: Behind the bar
dialogs.text: Welcome to the Lantern. Bed's three coppers, stew's two, and whatever rumor you came in chasing — sit down first and let me look at you before I decide if I've heard of it.

dialogs.title: When asked about the dragon
dialogs.text: Thirteen nights of fire on the high slopes. Caravans turning back. The Hollow guard riding double shifts. You don't need me to tell you what's coming. You need me to tell you who'll stand when it gets here, and the list is shorter every week.

dialogs.title: When asked about the Stranger in Grey
dialogs.text: He pays. He doesn't drink. He doesn't make trouble. Whoever he's waiting on, I hope they come soon — for his sake and mine.

npcs.name: Mira Hask
npcs.personal_history: Mira came up the dragon road from the southern coast twelve years back, set up a stall, and outlasted three rivals by being honest, sharp-elbowed, and impossible to outwait. She buys torches in bulk, weighs healing herbs to the half-leaf, and is the only merchant in Hollowmere still willing to extend credit — which she records in a small black book she will absolutely come looking for.

dialogs.title: At the counter
dialogs.text: Torches, picks, herbs, the usual. Caravan didn't come in this month so prices are up — don't argue with me, argue with the dragon.

dialogs.title: Asking for credit
dialogs.text: I'll write your name in my book. You don't want me to come looking for that name, friend. People who owe Mira Hask money have a way of finding the coin.

npcs.name: Captain Halvor Stiel
npcs.personal_history: Halvor took command of the Hollowmere watch the year the chapel bell cracked. Twenty-six guardsmen on the roster, nineteen still drawing pay, four who've stopped showing up since the fires on the slopes began. He drills the remaining fifteen at dawn in the chapel yard and pretends not to notice when the smith brings them bread. He is going to die on this road and he has made his peace with it, and he would prefer the party not make a fuss.

dialogs.title: On the wall
dialogs.text: Halvor Stiel, captain of the Hollow guard. Whatever you came up the road for, if it brings trouble to my walls, you'll answer to me first and the dragon second.

dialogs.title: Recruiting the party
dialogs.text: I've got fifteen guardsmen and a wyrm on the mountain. If you can fight, and you'd rather fight up there than down here, the road to the peaks is open and the gate will be left unbarred.

npcs.name: Acolyte Tomas
npcs.personal_history: Tomas was orphaned by the road sickness two winters ago and taken in by Elder Marisol when nobody else would feed another mouth. He tends the chapel candles, copies prayer books in a cramped careful hand, and is afraid of the Wandering Wood in a quiet steady way that he refuses to admit. Marisol is teaching him the healing rites, and he is a better student than he believes.

dialogs.title: At the chapel door
dialogs.text: Elder Marisol is in the inner sanctuary. I can take a message, if you'd like — or you can wait. She doesn't mind being interrupted, only being lied to.

dialogs.title: Asked about the shuttered side chapel
dialogs.text: We don't open that one. Marisol boarded it up the night her sister vanished, and she hasn't been back in. I light a candle on the threshold every dusk. Just in case.

npcs.name: Calla
npcs.personal_history: Calla is nine years old and the daughter of Joren Vale, a charcoal-burner who walked into the Wandering Wood eight days ago to bring back his missing dog and has not come out. She lives with Brenna at the inn now, sweeps the common room, and waits at the western gate every dusk because she is the only person in Hollowmere who still expects her father to come home.

dialogs.title: At the western gate
dialogs.text: Are you going into the wood? My da went in to find Tally — that's our dog — and he hasn't come back. He's tall, and he has a burn on his left arm from the kiln. If you see him, will you tell him Calla is waiting?

dialogs.title: When her father is returned
dialogs.text: (She doesn't say anything. She just runs.)

npcs.name: Old Greaves
npcs.personal_history: Nobody in Hollowmere remembers Greaves's given name, including Greaves. He fought in the eastern campaign alongside Orin, came home with one ear and a permanent thirst, and has held down the corner stool at the Bent Lantern for as long as anyone can prove. He talks too loudly, lies pleasantly about his old battles, and — when he's three ales deep and somebody actually listens — tells the truth about the binding ritual he says his grandmother saw scratched into a stone in the Auric ruins.

dialogs.title: First ale
dialogs.text: Buy me a round, and I'll tell you a true thing. Buy me three, and I'll tell you a true thing worth dying over.

dialogs.title: Third ale
dialogs.text: The Auric kings didn't kill the wyrm. They couldn't. They chained it — the chain's carved in the floor of the deepest hall in the old ruins. Whoever broke it broke us all, and I'd bet my last copper it wasn't a stranger.

npcs.name: Wenn the Boglark
npcs.personal_history: Wenn keeps a turf-roofed hut at the edge of the Wandering Wood, gathers herbs the chapel won't touch, and is one of perhaps three people in living memory to walk into the wood and walk back out. She is courteous, slightly cracked, and entirely unwilling to say what she saw in there. She trades with Mira for salt and with Marisol for nothing at all.

dialogs.title: At her hut
dialogs.text: You've come a long way for a leaf. Sit. The kettle's hot. The wood is listening, so we'll speak of small things first.

dialogs.title: Asked about the wood
dialogs.text: It isn't haunted. Haunted is a small word. The wood is somebody, and that somebody is older than the dragon, older than the Auric Throne, older than the names we use for old things. Bring iron. Bring salt. Don't bring fire.

npcs.name: Lyra Vance
npcs.personal_history: Lyra rode in two weeks ago on a horse worth more than the inn, paid a month's lodging in advance, and has been asking very specific questions about the dragon's range, sleeping patterns, and prior bindings. She introduces herself as a sellsword. She is in fact contracted by a southern lord who would prefer the dragon dead before any local hero claims the bounty. She is not unfriendly, only direct, and she will let the party do the hard part if they let her.

dialogs.title: Across the common room
dialogs.text: You've got the look of people about to do something stupid for the right reasons. Sit down. I've got coin, a map of the lair, and a reason to share both.

dialogs.title: The offer
dialogs.text: My employer pays the bounty on the wyrm, no questions about who struck the killing blow. Walk in with me, walk out richer. The catch is that I leave before the dragon does, and you cover the retreat. Fair?

npcs.name: Edda of the Iron Pendant
npcs.personal_history: Marisol's younger sister. Vanished into the Wandering Wood nineteen years ago and is still nineteen years old. Whatever the wood gave back in exchange for keeping her is no longer entirely Edda, but the iron pendant at her throat is the same one Marisol wears beneath her vestments, and she remembers — when pressed — the name of the village she was born in. She is a discovered NPC, found only in the deeper levels of the wood, and she may be brought home, freed, or left where the wood placed her.

dialogs.title: When first encountered
dialogs.text: I know you. No — I know the road you came up. Are the chapel candles still lit? Is my sister still angry with me?

dialogs.title: Asked what she is
dialogs.text: I am what the wood agreed to leave of me. I am still Edda, mostly. I would like to see Marisol once before I am not.

npcs.name: Skarn the Crooked
npcs.personal_history: Chieftain of the goblin warrens beneath the lower Brimspire. Skarn earned his name from a spine broken in a rockslide and reset wrong by a clan healer; the cane he leans on is human thighbone and an old joke. He is not loved by his clan, only feared, and he has spent the past year cramming three more clans into his warrens as the dragon drives them down from the high passes. He is open to bribery, hates the dragon as much as anyone in the vale, and would happily watch the party die first.

dialogs.title: At the throne
dialogs.text: Big people in my tunnels. Big people with weapons. Skarn likes big people who bring presents. Skarn doesn't like the other kind. Which kind are you?

dialogs.title: Offered a bribe
dialogs.text: Pretty. Shiny. Fine. Skarn lets you pass. Skarn even points you at the deep door. But if you come back this way, you come back with the dragon's tooth, or you don't come back this way at all.

npcs.name: Warlord Murgath
npcs.personal_history: Murgath holds the Iron Mines with two hundred orcs and the bones of the last human foreman nailed above the gate. He is older than orcs are usually allowed to get, which means he is cleverer than orcs are usually allowed to be. He picked the deep galleries because the dragon's roar doesn't reach them, and he will fight any creature — wyrm, party, or rival warlord — that tries to take the mountain from him before he's ready to leave it.

dialogs.title: At the mine gate
dialogs.text: You came up the dragon's road to die in my mine? Fine. Fine. Better here than out there. At least the rock will remember you.

dialogs.title: If parley is offered
dialogs.text: Talk, then. I have time. The dragon has time. The mountain has more time than any of us. Make your words good ones.

npcs.name: Vael the Hollow-Eyed
npcs.personal_history: Last knight of the Auric Throne, sworn to the binding of the dragon, dead these eleven centuries and still walking the lowest hall of the old ruins. Vael was one of the seven who carved the chain into the stone of the deep floor; the breaking of that chain unmade him in the same instant it freed the wyrm. He is no longer angry, only bound to the duty he failed, and he will help any party that means to put the wyrm back into the dark — provided they understand what binding costs.

dialogs.title: In the deep hall
dialogs.text: You walk on the carved floor. You see the broken chain. You smell what's left of me. Speak quickly: are you here to finish what we began, or merely to loot what we died for?

dialogs.title: Asked about the binding
dialogs.text: The chain is not a chain. It is a name held by seven willing throats. Six of us are dust. The seventh waits in a back room above the Bent Lantern, and he has waited long enough.

npcs.name: Aurigax, the Brimspire Wyrm
npcs.personal_history: Aurigax slept under the Brimspire for eleven hundred years, bound by the seven-throat chain of the Auric Throne, and woke last spring when the chain was broken. He is gold-and-rust scaled, polite in the way very old things sometimes are, and he does not particularly want the vale — he wants the sky, and the vale is in the way. He will speak with the party before he kills them. He has been told it is courteous. He is not above being lied to and he is not above being chained again, but the second binding will cost more than the first.

dialogs.title: Granted an audience
dialogs.text: Small ones. You climbed a long road to stand in my smoke. Speak. I am told it is the polite thing, before the burning.

dialogs.title: Asked to leave the vale
dialogs.text: I left the vale alone for an age and an age. The vale did not return the courtesy. Bring me the throat that broke my chain and I will consider going back to sleep. Bring me anything less and I will consider you breakfast.

npcs.name: Sela Varn
npcs.personal_history: Sela is the third Varn to keep the post's ledgers and the first to keep them alone. Her grandmother founded Varnfell on a handshake with a ship captain who never missed a season; her father drowned bringing a late cargo around the point; her brother Edric took the last shipment south down the tradeway two months ago and sent back one note: 'wolves.' She still opens the shutters every morning at first light, because a trading post that looks closed is a trading post that is closed.

dialogs.title: At the counter
dialogs.text: Varn and Daughters, est. before you were born. Torches, rope, herbs, ore if you're buying, furs if you're mad. Prices are fair because there's nobody left to undercut me.

dialogs.title: Asked about the empty harbor
dialogs.text: Two seasons, no sails. First we blamed the weather. Then the wrecks started washing up — cargo lashed tight, crews gone. Maro can show you. I don't go down to the sand anymore.

dialogs.title: Asked about her brother
dialogs.text: Edric took six sledges down the tradeway in the autumn and made it as far as the second ridge. The wolves down there don't behave like wolves. He swears something in the old delve is feeding them, and my brother does not scare easy.

npcs.name: Doran Pike
npcs.personal_history: Doran was bosun on the Levant Star when she broke her back on the Varnfell sand forty years ago. He waded ashore, looked at the wreck, looked at the snow, and decided he'd been going the wrong direction his whole life. He built the Driftwood Hearth out of her timbers and has kept the fire lit every night since — partly for the cold, mostly as a signal to any ship still out there that somebody on this coast is home.

dialogs.title: By the fire
dialogs.text: Sit. Stew's hot, beds are dry, and the fire's older than most of the people in this town. You've got the look of somebody who came north on purpose, which makes you the most interesting thing to walk in here all winter.

dialogs.title: Asked about the hearth
dialogs.text: Forty years, never let it die. When the ships ran, they'd steer by the glow. Ships are gone now, but I figure — the night I let it go out is the night the north decides we've given up. Not on my watch.

dialogs.title: Asked about the Frost Delve
dialogs.text: Prospectors dug it before my time, gave it up when the ore quit. Henna's the one to ask — she's been up at the entrance every week, muttering about warm air. Warm air, in this country. That's not a draft, friend. That's a door open somewhere it shouldn't be.

npcs.name: Ibsen Cole
npcs.personal_history: Ibsen has run traplines out of Varnfell for twenty years and knows every wolf within three days' walk by its gait. That's how he knows the packs on the tradeway are wrong: they're too big, too patient, and they ignore the deer. Wolves that don't eat are wolves that answer to something. He's lost two traplines and one good dog finding that out, and he has personally stopped going south without iron in hand.

dialogs.title: Near the south gate
dialogs.text: You'll be wanting the tradeway south. So does every fur and ounce of ore in this town. Problem is the wolves got there first, and these aren't wolves you wave a torch at.

dialogs.title: Asked about the packs
dialogs.text: Twenty years I've trapped this country. Wolves keep to the deer runs and mind their own hunger. These sit on the road. They watch. A pack that doesn't eat is a pack that's been put there, you understand me? Put there.

npcs.name: Maro Tides
npcs.personal_history: Maro was born in Varnfell, which makes him rare, and never wanted to leave, which makes him unique. He fished the point until the fish went strange and now walks the sand every dawn, logging what the sea sends back: ship timbers, lashed crates, a wheel with no ship attached. He keeps the log in pencil in a sailcloth notebook, because somebody should be writing this down, and nobody else volunteered.

dialogs.title: On the sand
dialogs.text: Mind the tideline — that's where I do my reading. The sea's been sending us mail with no return address. Crates, spars, a binnacle still polished. Everything but the sailors.

dialogs.title: Asked about the wrecks
dialogs.text: Week back, a crate came in south of here, past the rocks. Trade-sealed, heavy, sitting on the sand pretty as you please. I'd have hauled it up myself, but something's been pacing the shore down there at night, and I read better than I fight.

npcs.name: Henna Stone
npcs.personal_history: Henna swung a pick in the Frost Delve for nine years before the brimite veins ran dry and the company pulled out. She stayed — partly for the quiet, partly because she never believed the delve was empty, only finished with them. Lately she's been proven right in the worst way: the entrance breathes warm air, the snow won't settle on the ridge, and the sounds from below aren't echoes, because echoes answer you back in your own voice.

dialogs.title: Watching the ridge
dialogs.text: Nine years I worked that delve. Cold as a debt collector's heart, every level of it. Now it sighs warm air like something's sleeping at the bottom. I'm too old to go down and check. You're not.

dialogs.title: Asked what's below
dialogs.text: We stopped at two levels because the ore stopped. But the survey crew always said the cracks kept going — down past where the lamps made sense. If something's come up from that far under, I want to know what it is before it wants to know about us.

npcs.name: Elder Bryn Oakhallow
npcs.personal_history: Bryn is the eleventh grove-keeper of Elderbough, sworn to the treaty his ancestors cut with the Greymantle Circle: the town takes deadfall only, shares salt at the tree-ring, strikes no flame inside it — and in return the Bough-Wife keeps the forest's patience on Elderbough's side. For sixty years the keeping was ceremony. Since the spring the wyrm woke, it has become work. The heart-tree drops leaves out of season, the spring runs cold then warm then cold, and the Bough-Wife — who slept a season at a time when Bryn was young — has not slept at all. She says something below the roots is counting, and that the count has nearly reached the Wood she was cut from.

dialogs.title: At the tree-ring
dialogs.text: Welcome to Elderbough, travelers. Sheathe the iron, share the salt — there's the bowl, it's good manners and binding law in the same gesture. You've come at a strange season. All the seasons are strange now, and the lady of our grove has stopped sleeping through any of them.

dialogs.title: Asked about the treaty
dialogs.text: Eleven generations ago the Circle planted a cutting of the Wandering Wood here — a piece of the old Wood that agreed, for reasons no record explains, to live among people. We keep her terms: deadfall only, salt shared, no flame in the ring. She keeps the forest from remembering that towns are made of dead trees. It is a better arrangement than most realms have with their old powers, and I intend to die having kept it.

dialogs.title: Asked why the spirit doesn't sleep
dialogs.text: She says it plainly, when she says anything: something far below is going door to door among the old powers, checking each lock in turn. The Wood she was cut from has a door. She does not — she's a cutting, planted free, never bound. So she lies awake wondering which is worse: to be counted, or to be the one thing the counter finds unaccounted for.

npcs.name: The Bough-Wife
npcs.personal_history: The Bough-Wife is the spirit of Elderbough's heart-tree — a living cutting of the Wandering Wood, planted by the Greymantle Circle eleven generations ago and grown into something the old doctrine has no category for: an Elder's child raised among people. She wears a shape like a woman when she wants conversation and no shape at all when she doesn't. She is not bound, not sealed, and not listed in any Auric ledger, which made her a curiosity in quiet times. The times are not quiet. The counting moving beneath the old seals has passed under her roots twice now, slow and methodical, and both times it paused — the way a steward pauses at a door that has no number. She has begun teaching Bryn things grove-keepers were never taught, in the manner of someone setting affairs in order.

dialogs.title: Beneath the heart-tree
dialogs.text: You smell of roads, iron, and other people's quarrels. Sit anyway. The Wood I was cut from would have kept you; I only keep apples. Ask what you came to ask — I have been awake for four hundred nights and conversation is the one good use I've found for them.

dialogs.title: Asked about the counting
dialogs.text: Twice it has passed under me. Not footsteps — accounting. Every old thing in this land has a door and a lock and a number, and something is walking the ledger, checking each one. It paused at me, little ones. I have no door. I was planted free, a cutting given to people as a wedding-gift between the Wood and the world. Do you know what a careful steward does with an entry that fits no column? Neither do I. That is why I don't sleep.

dialogs.title: Asked how to help
dialogs.text: Keep my grove clean and my treaty kept, and I am stronger — old things are mostly made of being remembered correctly, and I am remembered by one small town. Beyond that: when you go down into the warm dark — and you will, you have the look — notice things for me. What the counter touches. What it skips. Whether the skipped things looked relieved. Bring me that, and I will owe you a season of good apples and one honest answer.

npcs.name: Tansy Mosswane
npcs.personal_history: Tansy keeps Elderbough's stillroom, third of her name to do it, and is cousin to Korrigan Mosswane who speaks for the Greymantle Circle — a family connection she describes as 'useful at solstice, insufferable at supper.' She physics the town, provisions the wardens, and reads the forest's health the way Maro Tides reads the tideline: by what turns up. What's turning up is wrong. Web in the warden-trees with no honest spider's pattern to it, roots gone black and bitter where the soil was sweetest, and her simples losing strength as if the green itself were distracted. Her cousin's circle calls it sympathy-sickness: when an old power frets, everything that grew in its shade frets with it.

dialogs.title: In the stillroom
dialogs.text: Mind the racks — everything hanging is either medicine or dinner and I'd rather not relabel. Salves, tinctures, a tea for road-feet that actually works. And if you're the capable-looking sort, stay a moment, because the grove is sick in a way my pots can't reach and my pride just finished arguing about asking for help.

dialogs.title: Asked about the blight
dialogs.text: Web in the warden-trees, spun wrong — too regular, like script. Blight-root underneath, black and bitter, in soil my grandmother called the sweetest in the Reach. It isn't disease, it's distraction: the lady's awake and frightened, and the green frets with her. Cut the spinners out, dig the root, and the grove can put its strength back where it belongs. Iron's allowed for this — the treaty makes exceptions for surgery.

npcs.name: Garrick Thornholt
npcs.personal_history: Garrick wardens the forest bounds of Elderbough — the town's voice on the trails and the forest's voice at the moot, a job that mostly means walking, counting game, and knowing which silences are normal. The silences stopped being normal in the spring. The packs his father taught him to read have gone wrong the way Varnfell's wolves went wrong: sitting where nothing feeds, watching what nothing watches. Something big has denned at the sister-spring two days south, fouling water the grove shares roots with, and last new moon Garrick cut a troll's track moving under the boughs with wolves walking escort — wolves escorting a troll, which his father's woodcraft has no page for. He has stopped patrolling alone, and Garrick Thornholt has never in his life patrolled with company.

dialogs.title: By the south gate
dialogs.text: You came up the forest road and nothing followed you — I know, I watched it not happen, which these days is the strangest thing I've seen all week. Garrick Thornholt, warden. If you can use those blades in tree-cover, the moot will pay you, the lady will thank you, and I will personally stop being the only person in this town who knows how bad it's gotten.

dialogs.title: Asked what's in the forest
dialogs.text: Packs that sit the trails like sentries and don't eat. A den at the sister-spring with kills around it nothing's fed on. And one track I'll say quietly: troll, moving with wolves at heel — escorted, like it had somewhere to be and rank enough to be walked there. My father's craft says trolls den alone and wolves serve nothing. The forest's rewriting the book, and I'd like armed friends while I read it.

npcs.name: Petra Alderwood
npcs.personal_history: Petra keeps the Moot Hall — inn, courthouse, and council chamber in one timbered room, which makes her innkeep, bailiff, and clerk of Elderbough depending on the hour. Her family raised the hall from a single storm-felled oak eleven generations back, with the Bough-Wife's blessing carved over the door in script nobody living can read. Petra pours fair measures, keeps the moot's minutes in a hand like bird-tracks, and enforces the hall's one absolute rule — grievances stay at the table, never follow anyone out the door — with a stare that has ended feuds the courts of the capital couldn't touch.

dialogs.title: Behind the long counter
dialogs.text: Welcome to the Moot Hall — inn this side of the counter, courtroom that side, and the kitchen outranks both. Beds are two coppers, the stew is whatever the forest allowed this week, and if you're here on a moot night you'll get supper and self-government at no extra charge.

dialogs.title: Asked about the script over the door
dialogs.text: The lady's blessing, carved when the hall was raised from one storm-felled oak — her gift, since the treaty doesn't let us cut. Nobody reads the script anymore, but Bryn says it's not words exactly. It's a name held in wood. The hall's never burned, never leaked, never settled an inch in eleven generations, so whatever it says, I dust it weekly and keep my theories respectful.

npcs.name: Foreman Dann Skell
npcs.personal_history: Skell came north with a timber contract, six axemen, and the firm opinion that trees are lumber that hasn't been invoiced yet. He set a camp two days south of Elderbough — outside the town's bounds, he'll note, entirely legal — and dropped nine old-growth warden-trees before the forest answered. What answered didn't leave tracks his men would stay to describe: the camp emptied in a night, the contract is void, and Skell alone refused to run, out of some sediment of stubbornness he's since had time to examine. He sits at Elderbough's edge now, tolerated rather than welcomed, paying his debt the only way the moot would accept: naming every tree he felled at the tree-ring on salt-days, and telling every southbound logger exactly why the Reach's timber isn't worth the wages.

dialogs.title: At the town's edge
dialogs.text: Go ahead, the look's free — I'm the idiot who brought axes to the Reach. Nine warden-trees, contract-legal, every cut outside the town bounds. And then the forest sent something to explain the difference between legal and permitted, and my crew found religion and the southern road in the same hour. I stayed. Somebody had to answer for it, and the axes were mine.

dialogs.title: Asked about his debt
dialogs.text: The moot wouldn't take coin — the lady doesn't spend it. So every salt-day I stand at the tree-ring and name them. Nine trees, oldest first; Bryn taught me their names and I don't get to write them down. Eleven salt-days done. The lady hasn't spoken to me once. But last time, an apple dropped at my boot — sour, mind you. Bryn says that's how forgiveness starts: unripe.

npcs.name: Captain Hesta Morn
npcs.personal_history: Hesta commands the Lastlight watch, third captain since the crack opened and the first to last more than two years. Her predecessors died of the two classic captain's errors — going down the crack to settle it, and pretending it could be ignored — and she has built her whole command on refusing both. Her doctrine fits on the gate plaque: the wall stands, the lamps burn, the warding line gets new stones before the old ones crack, and nobody is a hero on her shift. Since the spring the wyrm woke, the arithmetic has turned against her: the dead in the watch-yard stir more often, the imps come up in threes where they came up alone, and her requisitions to the Knight-Marshal come back marked 'noted.'

dialogs.title: At the south gate
dialogs.text: Lastlight. Yes, the lamps are on at noon — read the plaque. I'm Morn, captain of this wall, and if you're the sellsword kind I have three jobs and no patience for negotiating, because everything that comes out of that crack negotiates better than you do.

dialogs.title: Asked about the town
dialogs.text: Three captains in twelve years. The first went down the crack with twenty good soldiers and is presumably still going down. The second decided it was a geological feature and died surprised. I hold the wall, I light the lamps, I replace the stones. It's not glory. It's the reason there's still a town behind me to be unimpressed by it.

npcs.name: Mother Halvane
npcs.personal_history: Halvane keeps the Chapel of the Vigil and its one unbroken rite: every name in the watch-yard read aloud nightly, oldest first, no nights off. The Vigil's doctrine descends from the same root as Mournfield's observance — the dead stay down while they are remembered correctly — but Lastlight's version has teeth, because here the doctrine is tested. The month a fever took her voice, the watch-yard opened twice; a novice finished the readings and the ground went quiet. Halvane has read every night since, through frost and siege-nights, and keeps the chapel's name-ledger with the care of a woman who knows exactly what each forgotten line costs. Lately the readings take longer. Not because the list grows — because something below has started listening, and she refuses to rush for it.

dialogs.title: In the chapel
dialogs.text: Softly, traveler — the names from last night are still settling. This is the Vigil: every soul in the watch-yard, read aloud, every night, oldest first. You may think it's mourning. It is masonry. The wall keeps out what climbs. The reading keeps down what remembers.

dialogs.title: Asked about the rite
dialogs.text: Mournfield keeps candles; we keep names — same treaty, older terms. But something has changed since the spring. I read, and the quiet under the floor has the shape of attention now. It is checking my list against its own, do you understand? Somewhere below there is a ledger of our dead, and the night the two disagree, I want it to be because mine is more complete.

npcs.name: Odo Marsh
npcs.personal_history: Odo held a wall-post for eleven years before an imp's claw took the tendons of his shield arm, and the watch pension bought him the inn. He renamed it The Last Lamp, hung his old shield behind the bar, and runs the place as an extension of the wall: watch members drink at cost, rooms face inward, and the lamp over the door draws from the same oil ration as the gate-lights — Odo argued it into the town charter himself. He hears everything worth hearing in Lastlight by the second tankard, and has an old soldier's exact sense of which rumors go to the captain, which to the chapel, and which die at his bar.

dialogs.title: Behind the bar
dialogs.text: The Last Lamp — beds inward, stew's hot, and the lamp out front burns on the town's oil because I shamed the charter committee into it. Eleven years on that wall before an imp redecorated my arm, so if you're here to work the captain's jobs, your first round's mine. Tradition.

dialogs.title: Asked for news
dialogs.text: Wick-boy says the north lamps are burning blue at the bottom of the glass, which means the air from the crack's gotten richer. The scholar in the corner has bought the same room for forty nights and writes facing the door. And Brike's been selling fewer salvage trinkets and drinking more, which from her is a weather report. Draw your own conclusions. Mine's behind the bar with a strap I can pull one-armed.

npcs.name: Magister Ilex Corven
npcs.personal_history: Ilex held the university's chair of infernal taxonomy for nineteen years without ever meeting his subject, then resigned the week the survey reports from the cracks crossed his desk. He has lodged at The Last Lamp for forty nights, paying in coin and warnings, and his monograph-in-progress — 'On the Lesser Emanations' — is the only systematic study of the imps anywhere in the realm. His findings unsettle the watch more than the imps do: the things are not invading, they are surveying. They take nothing, eat nothing, and die without complaint — but every one that gets past the wall is found near the chapel, the watch-yard, or the warding line. They are, Ilex insists, checking the locks from the outside. He needs specimens stopped mid-errand to prove it, and he is too old to catch them himself.

dialogs.title: At the corner table
dialogs.text: Sit, sit — mind the papers, they're in taxonomic order. Ilex Corven, formerly of the university, presently of the only town in the realm where my discipline has fieldwork. You've seen the little horrors on the road, I expect. Tell me everything: gait, grouping, what they were looking at. Especially what they were looking at.

dialogs.title: Asked about the imps
dialogs.text: Nineteen years I taught that imps were vermin — the gnats of the pit. Then I came here and watched one ignore a full grain-store to stand for an hour in front of the chapel, looking. They don't raid, traveler. They inspect. Something below is using its smallest servants to walk our defenses, and the conclusion I keep not writing down is this: you only survey a wall you intend, eventually, to come through.

npcs.name: Brike
npcs.personal_history: Brike went down the Near Crack on a dare at sixteen and came back up three days later with a sack of grave-goods, a streak of white hair, and a permanent unwillingness to discuss days two and three. She has made her living off the crack's edges since — salvaging what the first watch dropped when it fell, selling trinkets and map-scraps to anyone with coin and no sense — and she knows the upper dark better than anyone living, precisely because she has never once gone past the second turning again. Lately her trade has dried up by her own choice: the upper dark has gotten crowded, the imps have stopped ignoring her, and on her last trip she found one of her own old chalk-marks rubbed out and redrawn. Facing the other way.

dialogs.title: Near the sealed house
dialogs.text: You've got crack-curiosity all over you. Fine — Brike, salvage and intelligence, semi-retired as of recently. I know the upper dark to the second turning better than the captain's maps do, and my rates are fair because the information is genuinely worth dying for. That's not a figure of speech. It's the price history.

dialogs.title: Asked why she stopped
dialogs.text: Sixteen years I've marked my routes in the upper dark — my chalk, my code, my hand. Last trip, my mark at the second turning was gone. Rubbed out. And next to it, fresh, my own sign — drawn backward, pointing in. Something down there learned to read me, friend, and then it wrote back. A person can retire on that. I have.

npcs.name: Tobb the Wick
npcs.personal_history: Tobb is Lastlight's lamplighter — a halfling with a striker-pole twice his height, a ring of oil-keys, and the only civilian post in town the watch salutes. The charter lists thirty-one lamps; Tobb maintains thirty-three, having quietly added two of his own over the watch-yard, paid out of his wage. He walks the full circuit twice nightly, knows every lamp's temper — which ones gutter in a north wind, which burn blue when the crack exhales — and reads the town's danger off the flames the way Ibsen Cole reads wolf-sign. The watch logs say 'all lamps lit' in Tobb's careful hand every night for nine years, with one exception he reported himself: the night of the spring equinox, when every flame in town leaned north for the space of ten breaths, toward the crack, as if something had inhaled.

dialogs.title: On the lamp round
dialogs.text: Mind the pole — oil's dear and you're wearing boots I'd hate to ruin. Tobb, lamplighter, thirty-three lamps and every one of them my personal acquaintance. You want to know how the town's doing on any given night, don't ask the watch. Ask the flames. The watch only knows what's happened. The lamps know what's coming.

dialogs.title: Asked about the equinox
dialogs.text: Nine years, one irregularity, and I logged it myself: spring equinox, the night the chain broke out west — though we didn't know that yet. Every lamp in Lastlight leaned north. Ten breaths. Then they stood back up and burned like nothing happened. Flames lean toward air, traveler. Something below the crack took a breath that night, and it hasn't let it out yet. I count my lamps. I'd appreciate you keeping anything from adding them to a different ledger.

dialogs.title: The King's Message
dialogs.text: Seek out King Wellerman in the Capital! We are under attack and need to muster every adventurer in the realm now!
